sections.title_en: The General Principle of the Laws of Mixtures
sections.body_en:
There are two fundamental rules in the law of forbidden foods that became mixed with permitted foods. The first rule: bitul be-shishim (nullification in sixty): if the forbidden substance became mixed into a quantity whose volume is sixty times greater than it, its flavor is not perceptible, and the mixture is permitted to eat. For this is how the Sages estimated: if the permitted food contains sixty times the forbidden substance, it is known that the flavor of the forbidden substance is nullified, because even foods with a very strong flavor, such as onion, do not impart flavor in more than sixty times their amount (Ḥullin 97b, Ran and Ra'avya).

The second rule: bitul be-rov (nullification in a majority): if the forbidden food does not impart flavor to the mixture – one follows the majority. For example, a piece of tereifa meat that became mixed with two pieces of kosher meat like it – it is nullified in the majority, as it is stated (Shemot 23:2): “Incline after the majority” (SA 109:1; below section 8).

For the forbidden substance to impart flavor to the permitted food, two conditions must be met: first, that the mixture be min be-she'eino mino (a kind with a different kind), that is, that the flavor of the forbidden substance is different from the flavor of the permitted food, so that it can be perceived in it. Second, that the mixture be laḥ be-laḥ (liquid with liquid), for then the flavor of the forbidden substance blends into the mixture. For example: when milk becomes mixed into a meat soup, its flavor spreads through the soup. Likewise, when a piece of non-kosher meat is cooked with vegetables, the non-kosher flavor mixes into the vegetables.

But if one of the two conditions is not met, even though the forbidden and the permitted are mixed, the flavor of the forbidden substance does not spread into the permitted food. For example, if a piece of forbidden meat became mixed with two pieces of permitted meat whose flavor is different, even though this is a mixture of min be-she'eino mino, since the mixture is yavesh be-yavesh (dry with dry), the flavor of the forbidden substance does not pass into the permitted foods, and therefore by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority. Likewise, when gravy of tereifa meat became mixed with gravy of kosher meat, even though the mixture is laḥ be-laḥ and the forbidden substance blends into the permitted, since the flavor of the forbidden substance is like the flavor of the permitted, it does not impart flavor to it, and therefore by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority.

However, the Sages made a protective fence for the Torah and enacted that even when only one of the two conditions that enable the transfer of flavors is met – either it is a mixture of laḥ be-laḥ, or it is a mixture of min be-she'eino mino – the forbidden substance is not nullified in a majority, but sixty times is needed to nullify it (Rashba and Rosh). The Sages had another important aim in their enactment: to make the measures uniform, so that there would be a single law of nullification in sixty for all mixtures that resemble a mixture in which the forbidden substance can impart flavor (Ran). Therefore, even when the basis of the prohibition is rabbinic, we do not say that there is no need to make a fence for it; rather, sixty times is needed to nullify it, because the Sages made their measures uniform (Beit Yosef and Rema 109:1).1

notes_en.en: The basis of the rule that one follows the majority we learned from the laws of the court: when the judges disagree among themselves, one follows the majority, as it is stated (Shemot 23:2): “Incline after the majority” (Ḥullin 11a). The Sages learned a support for the rule of nullification in sixty from what is explained in the Torah: all the meat of the shelamim (peace-offering) sacrifice brought by the nazirite is cooked together with the foreleg that is given to the kohen, and even though the foreleg is forbidden to an Israelite to eat, it does not render the sacrificial meat forbidden to an Israelite, because the meat is sixty times greater than it (Ḥullin 98a).

sections.title_en: Summary of the Four Types of Mixtures
sections.body_en:
Thus there are two distinctions in the laws of mixtures: the first, min be-mino (a kind with its own kind) and min be-she'eino mino. In min be-mino the flavor of the forbidden substance is the same as the flavor of the permitted; in min be-she'eino mino the flavor of the forbidden substance is different from the flavor of the permitted.

The second: laḥ be-laḥ and yavesh be-yavesh. In laḥ be-laḥ the flavor of the forbidden substance blends into the mixture, such as non-kosher meat cooked with kosher meat, where through the cooking the flavors mix throughout the dish. Forbidden flour that became mixed with permitted flour is also considered a mixture of laḥ be-laḥ, since flour is fine and the forbidden and permitted particles blend into one another (Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 7:4). By contrast, in a mixture of yavesh be-yavesh we do not know which food is kosher and which is forbidden, but they do not blend into one another. A cup containing gravy of non-kosher meat that became mixed up with two cups containing gravy of kosher meat is also considered a mixture of yavesh be-yavesh, because the gravies are in separate cups and do not mix with one another.

Since the two distinctions combine with each other, there are four types of mixtures: a) min be-she'eino mino, laḥ be-laḥ; b) min be-she'eino mino, yavesh be-yavesh; c) min be-mino, laḥ be-laḥ; d) min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh.

In the first three types, sixty times is needed to nullify the forbidden substance. In the first, sixty times is needed by the essential law, because of the flavor the forbidden substance imparts to the mixture. In the second and third types, by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority, and the Sages enacted that it is not nullified in less than sixty. Only in a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh) is the practical halakha that the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority. Admittedly, some hold that the Sages made all the measures uniform and established that no forbidden substance is nullified in less than sixty times. However, in practice the halakha follows the opinion of most Rishonim, that a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh) is nullified in a majority, and this is the situation in which the fundamental rule of nullification in a majority applies.

However, specifically regarding a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh), when the prohibition has extra severity, the Sages were more stringent than with other mixtures, which are nullified in sixty. If the forbidden substance is teruma fruit that became mixed with ordinary fruit, since the prohibition of teruma has extra severity – a non-kohen who eats it is punishable by death [at the hands of Heaven] – the teruma fruit is nullified only if the ḥullin (non-sacred) fruit is a hundred times as much. And when the forbidden substance is orla fruit or kilei ha-kerem (mixed vineyard produce), which are forbidden even for benefit, the forbidden substance is nullified only if the permitted fruit is two hundred times as much (below, halakha 9).2

notes_en.en:
Some hold that the Sages made all the measures uniform and established that only when there is sixty times against the forbidden substance is it nullified by virtue of its extreme smallness, but if there is not sixty times against it, it has significance and has not yet been nullified from awareness. This is the opinion of the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:4-5), the Eshkol and the Ramban (Ḥullin 97b; and according to the Ra'avan, by Torah law it is not nullified in less than sixty). However, in practice the ruling follows the opinion of most Rishonim, that a mixture of the fourth type (min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh) is nullified in a majority, and this is the situation in which the fundamental rule of nullification in a majority applies. For this is the plain meaning of the Gemara (Ḥullin 99b), and so wrote Tosafot, the Terumah, Ra'avad, Rosh, Rashba, Ran, Semag, Meiri and many others.
In practice, in most cases of a min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh mixture, according to all opinions the nullification is in a hundred, for as emerges from the mishnayot, the common mixture of min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh was teruma fruit that became mixed with ḥullin fruit because they are entirely similar. And the common case of min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh about which there is a dispute whether it is nullified in a majority or in sixty is non-kosher meat that became mixed with kosher meat, or a piece of ḥelev (forbidden fat) among pieces of permitted fat; these cases are less common, because the forbidden parts that are not intended for eating are customarily thrown away, or at least separated completely from the other foods.
All that we learned, that min be-mino is nullified in a majority or in sixty, is according to the Sages; but according to Rabbi Yehuda, min be-mino is not nullified even in a thousand. For nullification is created through a clash between two kinds, and when they are of the same kind there is no clash, and since the name of the forbidden substance still applies to it, it is not nullified. However, according to the Sages, even though they are of the same kind, a clash is created between the forbidden and the permitted, and the permitted overpowers the forbidden and nullifies it (Menaḥot 22a; Ran, Nedarim 52a).

sections.title_en: Ta'am Ke-ikar and Nullification in Sixty
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, in any situation in which the flavor of the forbidden substance can be perceived in the mixture, the entire mixture is forbidden, because ta'am ke-ikar (“flavor is like the substance itself”). That is, the flavor of a food is considered like its substance. Therefore, even when the forbidden substance is small in quantity, and the permitted flavors are many and stronger than it, as long as the flavor of the forbidden substance is perceptible – the forbidden substance is not nullified in the mixture, and all of it is forbidden to eat. The Sages estimated that the flavors of all foods are nullified in sixty, because even foods whose flavor is strong, such as onion, impart flavor up to sixty times and no more. Therefore the Sages established that all forbidden substances that can impart flavor are nullified in sixty. The exception is spices, whose flavor is strong, and the permitted food must contain a much larger amount in order to nullify their flavor (below section 6).

Therefore, if a little milk fell into a meat soup, and the soup did not contain sixty times the milk – the soup is forbidden. And if the soup contained sixty times the milk, it is clear to us that the flavor of the milk is not perceptible and the soup is kosher. Everything cooking in the soup combines to nullify the milk that fell into it in sixty, including: meat, vegetables, water and bones. Even bones that have no flavor, since they too absorb the flavors in the dish, also combine toward the measure of sixty times with which the forbidden substance is nullified (SA 99:1).

Likewise, if a little ground non-kosher meat became mixed into vegetable patties, if the vegetables contain sixty times the meat, it is known that the flavor of the meat is nullified and the patties are kosher. And if there is not sixty times – the patties are forbidden. Likewise, if non-kosher meat fell into a vegetable soup, if the soup contained sixty times against it, the soup is kosher; however, since it is possible to remove the non-kosher meat, one must remove it, for as long as it is recognizable – only its flavor is nullified, while it itself is not nullified. And if the soup did not contain sixty times against it, even though the non-kosher meat is removed, since its flavor spread through the soup and there was not sixty times against it – the entire soup is forbidden.3

notes_en.en:
The source for ta'am ke-ikar is from the mitzva of the nazirite, for in addition to the prohibition of drinking wine, it is stated: “he shall not drink any steeping of grapes” (Bamidbar 6:3), that is, water that has the flavor of wine. The Sages learned from this that such is the law for all the prohibitions in the Torah: flavor is considered like the substance of the forbidden item. According to Rabbi Akiva, the learning is from the fact that the Torah commanded to purge the utensils of gentiles because of the flavor absorbed in them. Another example of this is from cooking meat with milk, where even the meat alone is forbidden because of the flavor of the milk absorbed in it (Pesaḥim 44b).
According to many Rishonim ta'am ke-ikar is from the Torah, among them: Halakhot Gedolot, Tosafot, Rabbeinu Tam, the Terumah, Razah, Ra'avad, Rosh, Semag, Meiri and Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit He-arokh 4:1). And some say that ta'am ke-ikar is rabbinic: Rambam, Rashi, Ramban, Ra'ah, Nimukei Yosef, Ran, Ritva (however, if the thing imparting the flavor has thick substance, such as ḥelev that melted inside the dish, even according to the Ramban, Ran and Ritva the prohibition is from the Torah). In practice, the ruling is that ta'am ke-ikar is from the Torah, as explained in the Tur and SA 98:2.
If the forbidden substance was nullified in sixty, and when people ate from the mixture they perceived its flavor, the mixture is forbidden (Rema 98:8). But as we have learned, the chance of this happening is nil. A rabbinic prohibition is also nullified in sixty, and only in a case of doubt is one lenient regarding it (SA 98:2; Shakh 98:7; 26).

sections.body_en:
Although we have learned that as a rule the forbidden substance is nullified in sixty, when it is a mixture of min be-she'eino mino, since the forbidden substance has a flavor different from the permitted, one may give a gentile the dish to taste. If he perceives the flavor of the forbidden substance – the dish is forbidden; and if he does not perceive it, even though the permitted food does not contain sixty times – the dish is permitted (Ḥullin 97a-b). For we have learned that the reason the Sages enacted that forbidden substances be nullified in sixty is that even foods whose flavor is strong, such as onion, impart flavor up to sixty times and no more. Thus foods whose flavor is less strong are nullified in less than sixty times. But as long as we have no way of checking this, the Sages enacted that the forbidden substance be nullified in sixty; but if a reliable gentile says that there is no forbidden flavor in the mixture, the food is kosher.

Admittedly, many are stringent and hold that even when it is not possible to perceive the flavor of the forbidden substance, whenever there is not sixty times against the actual substance of the forbidden item, the mixture is forbidden (Ramban, Rashba, Ra'ah and Ran). But in practice the ruling follows the opinion of those who hold that even when actual forbidden substance became mixed into kosher food, if a reliable gentile said that the food has no forbidden flavor, even though the permitted food does not contain sixty times against the forbidden substance, the mixture is kosher, because everything depends on flavor (Rambam, Tosafot, Rosh, Tur and SA 98:1).

Therefore, if milk fell into a meat dish, the gentile should taste the dish. If he perceives a dairy flavor in it – the dish is forbidden. And if he does not perceive it, even though the meat dish does not contain sixty times the milk – the dish is permitted. Likewise, if non-kosher meat fell into a vegetable dish, the gentile should taste the dish; if he perceives a meat flavor in it – the dish is forbidden. And if he does not perceive it, even though the dish does not contain sixty times the non-kosher meat – the dish is kosher.

However, the problem is that the gentile may deviate from the truth in order to please the Jew or to harm him; therefore they said that only if he speaks innocently (mesi'aḥ lefi tumo), that is, he does not know that his answer has halakhic significance, may one rely on him. And if he is a cook, one may tell him that it concerns a halakhic question, and since his profession requires discerning flavors, he will give an accurate answer so as not to harm his professional reliability (Rashba).4

notes_en.en:
It is explained in the Gemara, Ḥullin 97a, that when teruma became mixed with ḥullin, a kohen is given it to taste: if he perceives the flavor of the teruma – the dish is permitted to kohanim only, and if he does not perceive it – the dish is permitted to all Israel. But if a forbidden substance became mixed with a permitted one, one relies on a kefila Aramaa. A kefila is a gentile baker or cook. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:30), the Sages' intent was to give an example of a gentile who regularly tastes foods, but in truth one may rely on any gentile who is willing to take upon himself the responsibility of determining the flavor of the dish. According to the Meiri, only someone who is an expert in flavors, such as a cook, may determine this. According to Rashi and the Or Zaru'a, the expert must be speaking innocently, not knowing that his judgment has halakhic implications (Roke'aḥ; Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥullin 96b). This is because if he knew that his words had halakhic significance, perhaps he would deviate from the truth in order to cause the Jew to stumble or to please him.
And according to many Rishonim, if he is an expert, one may rely on him to be accurate in his answer, since he will not want to damage his professional reliability (Tosafot, s.v. samkhinan, and Ran). The Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit He-arokh 4:1) further explained that in truth any person can determine the flavor of the mixture, as evidenced by the fact that one relies on an ordinary kohen regarding teruma; but an ordinary gentile may deviate from the truth, and therefore one relies on him only when he speaks innocently. However, one may rely on a kefila even when he knows that it is a halakhic question, because he will not want to harm his professional reliability. And so it was ruled in Beit Yosef 98:1 and Shakh 2. This is not considered relying on the testimony of a gentile to permit a Torah prohibition, for it is not a matter of testimony but of clarifying reality, and it is something that will become clear when people taste the dish (see Shakh 2, Taz 2, Pri Ḥadash 2).
However, according to the Ramban, Rashba, Ran, Ra'ah and Ritva, only flavor is nullified in less than sixty on the basis of a kefila, such as non-kosher meat that fell into soup and was afterwards removed from it: since there is no actual forbidden substance in the soup, one may rely on a kefila, so that if there is no forbidden flavor there – the soup is permitted. But when the actual forbidden substance became mixed in, the forbidden substance is not nullified in less than sixty. This is because the Sages made their measures uniform, so that any mixture that can impart flavor is nullified in sixty. For otherwise it would turn out that precisely when the forbidden substance imparts flavor it is sometimes nullified in less than sixty, whereas in a mixture of min be-mino, laḥ be-laḥ, or min be-she'eino mino, yavesh be-yavesh, where by Torah law the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority, it is never nullified in less than sixty. (And according to Rashi and the Or Zaru'a, even flavor is not nullified in less than sixty, and even when there is sixty times, if there is a kefila Aramaa there, one must give it to him to check, and if he perceives the forbidden flavor – the mixture is forbidden. And according to the other poskim, indeed if there is forbidden flavor the mixture is forbidden, but if there is sixty times there is no need to check this, because the chance that the forbidden flavor will be perceived is nil.)
And according to the Rambam, Tosafot, Rosh, Semag and Meiri, even actual forbidden substance against which there is not sixty times is nullified when its flavor is not perceived. And since the dispute concerns a rabbinic law (because when the forbidden flavor is nullified, according to all opinions there is no Torah prohibition in the mixture), the halakha follows the lenient opinion. And so it was ruled in the Tur and SA 98:1. However, in practice the custom is not to rely on a gentile to nullify a forbidden substance in less than sixty, as explained in the next halakha, and only in a pressing situation does one rely on the gentile's tasting.

sections.title_en: The Practical Custom – Nullification in Sixty
sections.body_en:
Several of the great Rishonim in Ashkenaz wrote that the practical custom is not to rely on tasting by a gentile; rather, if the permitted food contains sixty times more than the forbidden substance – the mixture is kosher, and if it does not contain sixty times – the mixture is forbidden. Apparently, the poskim found that in practice it is difficult to rely on tasting the dish, because flavor is elusive, and at times it happened that a gentile answered that the dish had no meat flavor, and when the Jew ate from it, he found that it had a meat flavor. And at times there were people who perceived the forbidden flavor and people who did not perceive it. The definition of flavor is also unclear: whether it refers to perceiving the flavor of the forbidden substance itself, or also to a different flavor having been created in the dish as a result of the forbidden substance. Therefore some of the Rishonim ruled not to rely on tasting by a gentile, but rather that all forbidden substances be nullified in sixty. Over the years this custom spread to all communities, until in recent generations all Israel are accustomed to rely on nullification in sixty and not on tasting by a gentile (Rema 98:1; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2; 11).

However, in a pressing situation, when a reliable gentile says with complete certainty that the dish has no forbidden flavor, one may permit the dish.5

notes_en.en:
Several Rishonim wrote that the custom is not to rely on tasting by a gentile; rather, if there is sixty times – it is permitted, and if not – it is forbidden (Mordekhai, Agur). And the Rema 98:1 wrote that this is the practical custom. This custom also spread in the Sephardic communities, as written by: Radbaz, Pri Ḥadash, Shulḥan Gavoha, Ziv'ḥei Tzedek, Ben Ish Ḥai, Berit Kehuna, Kaf Ha-ḥayim (98:2; 11). Apparently, on the basis of experience they came to realize that tasting by a gentile raises doubts, because flavor is elusive and it is not always possible to determine with certainty whether it is perceptible, and perhaps there will be people who perceive it and people who do not; therefore they preferred to make the measures uniform and follow the rule of nullification in sixty, similar to what the Sages established regarding dry min be-she'eino mino and liquid min be-mino (above section 2). The Radbaz (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:29) and Sefer Ha-teruma (siman 48) wrote along these lines. It is also possible that over the years we have become more exacting, and human tasting, which is not precise by absolute measures, creates doubts in people's hearts (just as nowadays they ruled that one does not fulfill the obligation of Keri'at Shema in translation, because no translation is precise enough for us; see Peninei Halakha: Tefila 15:9, note 7. Likewise regarding the writing of STaM [Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot], where the principle is that the writing must be perfect, and the Aḥaronim were exacting and more stringent regarding the form of the letter, because only in this way is the writing considered perfect for us). It is further possible that over the generations people began to use more spices, and as a result the difficulty of distinguishing between flavors increased, and the custom spread not to rely on tasting by a gentile. Furthermore, we learned in the previous note that according to many of the great Rishonim, when actual forbidden substance became mixed with permitted food, one does not rely on flavor, but rather the permitted food must contain sixty times, and according to Rashi even flavor is not nullified in less than sixty. Since they found that in practice it is difficult to rely on tasting, they preferred to satisfy all the poskim and to act in accordance with them. And so wrote Rabbi Akiva Eiger 98:1; Pri Megadim, Siftei Da'at 29.
However, it seems that in a pressing situation one may rely on tasting by a gentile, provided that his answer is certain. For we have learned that one does not rely on him out of concern that he may deviate from the truth, especially when the flavor is unclear, and if people become accustomed to relying on him, they will become accustomed to entering into doubts. But when one relies on him only in a pressing situation, and only rarely, and only when his answer is certain – there is no concern (see Responsa Rema 54; Yabi'a Omer 8, YD 10).
One may rely on a Jew: if there was a pareve dish into which meat gravy became mixed, a Jew may taste the dish and decide whether it is pareve or meat (Pri Ḥadash). And some say that all this is be-di'avad, but le-khatḥila, as long as the pareve food does not contain sixty times, one should be stringent and consider the dish as meat (Shakh 96:5).
A dish into which gravy of nevela (meat of an animal not properly slaughtered) became mixed and which did not contain sixty times, and a Jew mistakenly tasted from it and afterwards said that he did not perceive the flavor of the nevela: some say that one relies on him that there is no forbidden flavor there and the dish is permitted (Rabbi Akiva Eiger), and some say that one does not rely on him, for since he did not know that he needed to taste and determine the halakha, he did not pay attention to examine properly whether there was a flavor of nevela there (Beit Yitzḥak). However, if many tasted and did not perceive the forbidden flavor, it is reasonable that according to all opinions one may rely on them (Maharsham 3:377).

sections.body_en:
A spice imparts flavor in more than sixty times its amount; therefore, if a forbidden spice became mixed into a food, as long as its flavor is perceptible it renders the entire food forbidden, even if the food is a thousand times greater than it or more (Rema 98:8).6

Regarding a forbidden substance that causes the mixture to change its form or its nature, the Sages were stringent and established that even if there is sixty times against it, it is not nullified, since its effect is evident in the mixture. Therefore, if the stomach lining of a nevela was placed in milk so that the enzymes in it would turn the milk into cheese, the cheese is forbidden, since it was curdled by means of nevela (above 30:6). Likewise, if dough was leavened with forbidden yeast, the dough is forbidden even if it contained sixty times against the yeast. Likewise, if by means of forbidden yeast or vinegar a honey drink or fruit drink was fermented and turned into an intoxicating beverage, the beverage is forbidden even if it contained sixty times against the yeast (SA and Rema 87:11).

If the forbidden substance did not have enough to impart flavor to the food or to curdle it, and only with the help of a permitted flavor or a permitted coagulant did it impart flavor to the food or curdle it – its law is like that of other forbidden substances, and whenever the food contains sixty times against the forbidden substance – the food is kosher (Rema ibid.). This rule is called: “zeh ve-zeh gorem (this and that both cause it) – it is permitted.”7

notes_en.en: According to those who hold that ta'am ke-ikar is rabbinic, their prohibition is rabbinic (above, note 3). And among those who hold that ta'am ke-ikar is from the Torah, some say that it is from the Torah (Ran, Ḥullin 35:5 [?], in the pages of the Rif), and some say that ta'am ke-ikar is from the Torah up to sixty times, but beyond that the prohibition is rabbinic, for the Torah did not forbid a faint flavor (Shakh 98:29). The Yad Yehuda (98, long commentary 23) explained that those who follow the view that ta'am ke-ikar is from the Torah do not disagree; rather, if the flavor of the spice itself is perceptible – the prohibition is from the Torah, as the Ran says, and if it only caused the intensification of other flavors – the prohibition is rabbinic. In practice, although we learned in the previous halakha that the custom is not to rely on tasting by a gentile, when a forbidden spice became mixed into food, because of the great loss involved the custom is to rely on a gentile, and one adds the opinion of those who hold that beyond sixty times in any case the flavor renders forbidden only by rabbinic law (Shakh ibid.; Ḥavot Da'at, Ḥiddushim 19).

In the Mishna, Avoda Zara 29b, it is explained that the cheese of gentiles is forbidden. According to one of the explanations in the Gemara there, 35a, the prohibition is because gentiles curdle cheeses with the stomach lining of a nevela, and anything that curdles is considered as if it were present in its original form (above 30:6). Some say that with all the significance of a coagulant, it does not have the power to render forbidden more than sixty times (Rabbeinu Tam, the Terumah and Semag). However, according to most Rishonim, any forbidden substance that curdles the food is not nullified even in a thousand (Ri Migash, Rambam, Rashba, Ran and others). According to most poskim the prohibition is rabbinic (Issur Ve-heter, Eshkol, Pri Ḥadash, Pri Megadim and many others), and some hold that it is from the Torah (Riaz and Ḥatam Sofer). If the forbidden substance could have imparted flavor by itself, even though the permitted substance also has the power to impart flavor by itself, according to most poskim the dish is forbidden (Taz, Pri Ḥadash, MB 442:25), and some permit it (Yad Yehuda, Yeshu'ot Yaakov).

sections.body_en:
A forbidden food that fell into a dish and spoiled its flavor – even though the dish does not contain sixty times against the forbidden substance, and the flavor of the forbidden substance is noticeable in the dish – since its flavor spoils the dish, it is nullified in a majority and does not render the dish forbidden, in accordance with the rule: “noten ta'am li-fgam (one that imparts a detrimental flavor) – is permitted.” And even when the forbidden substance itself is tasty, as long as it spoils the dish, the dish is permitted. The spoilage need not be such that because of it people would refrain from eating the dish; rather, whenever the forbidden substance spoiled the flavor of the dish – the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority and the dish is permitted. But if the forbidden substance neither spoiled the flavor of the dish nor improved it, as long as its flavor is noticeable, the dish is forbidden (Avoda Zara 67b; SA 103:1-2).

Some say that even when the forbidden substance adds to the quantity of the dish, to the point that the gain from the increased quantity exceeds the loss from the spoiling of the flavor, the dish is permitted. For the main thing is the flavor, and as long as the forbidden substance spoils the flavor of the dish, it is nullified in a majority (Rashba). And some say that since in practice there is a benefit from the forbidden substance that became mixed into the dish – the dish is forbidden (Ran). In practice, one should be stringent, and in a pressing situation one may be lenient (see SA 103:2; Ziv'ḥei Tzedek 12).

Noten ta'am li-fgam is permitted on condition that the forbidden food always imparted a detrimental flavor; but if at first it improved and afterwards spoiled, or at first spoiled and afterwards improved – it is forbidden (SA 103:2).8

notes_en.en:
Avoda Zara 67b; 68a: according to Rabbi Meir, the prohibition of eating applies even to foods that have spoiled and are not fit for human consumption, and therefore noten ta'am li-fgam renders forbidden. According to Rabbi Shimon, the prohibition of eating applies only to foods fit for human consumption, as it is stated (Devarim 14:21): “You shall not eat anything that dies of itself; you may give it to the stranger who is within your gates, that he may eat it” – thus the prohibition of nevela applies to what is fit to eat. And the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon. Some say that even by rabbinic law there is no prohibition in eating something unfit to eat (Ra'ah, Ran and Rashbatz), and some say that by rabbinic law there is a prohibition in this, because by deciding to eat it one has given it significance (Rambam, Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam). And the Aḥaronim agreed to this as halakha (Pri To'ar, Pri Megadim, MB 442:43). All this is when the food underwent a process that caused it to spoil; but a forbidden substance that is repulsive in itself, such as creeping creatures, is forbidden to eat by Torah law even when it is repulsive (Avoda Zara 68b; Rashba and Minḥat Kohen).
When, unintentionally, a forbidden food that had become spoiled from human consumption became mixed into a good food and does not spoil it, even though the majority of the mixture is of the forbidden food, since it was not mixed in intentionally, one did not come to give it significance, and therefore the mixture is permitted to eat (Minḥat Kohen 1:9). But if it was mixed in intentionally – it is forbidden (Ḥavot Da'at 103:1; Igrot Moshe 2, YD 23; Mishneh Halakhot 3:11). And there is one who says that since the forbidden substance became spoiled from human consumption, it no longer carries the prohibition of eating, and only because it is putrid is it forbidden to eat it because of bal teshaktzu (“you shall not make yourselves abominable”); therefore, if it is intentionally mixed into permitted food in a manner that there will no longer be abomination in eating it, it is permitted to eat it le-khatḥila (Pri Ḥadash YD 103:1).
When the forbidden substance imparts a detrimental flavor, it does not render forbidden even when the mixture is fit to eat. Some explain that this is because the spoiling forbidden substance is nullified in a majority, and therefore the mixture is permitted even when, on the whole, one benefits from the added quantity (Rashba, Torat Ha-bayit 4:1). And some explain that the spoiled forbidden substance is nullified because there is no benefit from it, and therefore if there is more benefit from the added quantity, it renders forbidden (Ran, Avoda Zara 67b).

sections.title_en: The Law of Dry with Dry, Same Kind
sections.body_en:
As we have learned (in halakha 2), a piece of tereifa meat that became mixed with two pieces of kosher meat whose flavor is the same – the tereifa piece is nullified in the majority of kosher pieces. The same law applies when five forbidden pieces became mixed with six permitted pieces like them: since the majority is permitted, the minority is nullified and the entire mixture is kosher (SA 109:1; Shakh 6).

And although by Torah law the forbidden piece was nullified in the majority and became like a permitted one, by rabbinic law it is forbidden to eat all the pieces together, for if one eats them together, it is clear that with each and every eating he will also eat of the forbidden substance; rather, he should eat piece after piece, and in this way with each and every eating he can say that he is not eating of the forbidden substance. Likewise, it is forbidden to cook all the pieces together, because the cooking mixes the flavors of all the pieces, so that with every eating he will be eating of all of them (Rashba). And some say that by rabbinic law it is forbidden for one person to eat all the pieces, even one after another; rather, it is permitted only for two people to eat them, and in this way each one can say that he himself did not eat of the forbidden substance (Semag). Le-khatḥila it is good to be stringent in accordance with this view.9

notes_en.en: There are five opinions about how one should act with a mixture of dry with dry, same kind: a) Since the forbidden piece is nullified in the majority of the permitted, it is treated as entirely permitted, and it is permitted to eat all the pieces of the mixture together, and even to cook them together (the Terumah, Roke'aḥ, Rosh, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Semak and Tur). b) Although by Torah law it is permitted for one person to eat them together, by rabbinic law he should not eat them together, so that with every eating he can say, “Now I am not eating a forbidden substance” (Rashba and Ran, and so wrote the SA 109:1-2 as an unattributed ruling). c) It is rabbinically forbidden for one person to eat all of them; rather, only two may do so, in a manner that each one can say that he did not eat of the forbidden substance (Semag, Hagahot Sha'arei Dura, and the opinion of “some say” in the SA; and the Rema wrote to act this way le-khatḥila), and there is one who says that one is obligated to act this way by Torah law (Tosafot Rid). d) Some hold that by the letter of the law it is permitted to eat them together, but it is good to be mehader and give a gentile the amount of the forbidden piece, so that in practice the Jew will not benefit from the forbidden substance, and he can even attribute it to the forbidden piece being the one that was given to the gentile, while he himself ate only the permitted ones (Maharam of Rothenburg). e) All the opinions mentioned so far follow the view of most Rishonim, who hold that min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh is nullified in a majority; however, according to the Rambam, Ramban and Eshkol, the Sages made their measures uniform and established that even in min be-mino, yavesh be-yavesh sixty is needed to nullify the forbidden substance (above, note 2). Be-di'avad, when they have already been cooked together, the Rema 109:2 wrote that in a case of loss one may rely on the Rosh and those who concur with him, and it seems that the Beit Yosef also agrees to this, for he cited his opinion in Bedek Ha-bayit, end of siman 109. And the mehadrin act in accordance with the Maharam.

sections.title_en: Things That Are Not Nullified in Sixty
sections.body_en:
All that we have learned, that forbidden substances are nullified in sixty, and sometimes in a majority, applies specifically to ordinary forbidden substances; but with forbidden substances that have an aspect of severity, the Sages were more stringent. There are forbidden substances regarding which the Sages were stringent that they not be nullified even in a thousand, and there are forbidden substances regarding which the Sages were stringent that they be nullified in a measure of a hundred or two hundred. We will learn the laws from the most severe to the most lenient:

The basis for forbidden substances being nullified in sixty is that relative to such a large quantity of permitted food, the forbidden substance is nullified by virtue of its extreme smallness, as evidenced by the fact that even its flavor is not noticeable in a quantity sixty times greater than it. But when the forbidden substance has extra severity or significance, even in a very large mixture its name is noticeable, and in a person's awareness it is not nullified. Therefore the Sages enacted that especially significant things are not nullified even in a thousand, and they are:
a) a beriya (a whole creature) (below section 10); b) a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed bah (a piece fit to serve to an honored guest) (below section 11); c) significant items that are counted (below section 12). All these forbidden substances are not nullified, whether they became mixed with their own kind or with a different kind.

They further enacted that ḥametz on Pesaḥ and the prohibition of idolatry, because of their extra severity, are not nullified even in a thousand, whether with their own kind or with a different kind (SA OḤ 447:1; YD 140:1; Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 7:1-2).

Forbidden spices render their mixture forbidden as long as their flavor is noticeable. Likewise, something that curdles the food is not nullified as long as its effect is noticeable (above halakha 6).

And there are two types of forbidden substances regarding which the Sages enacted that only if they became mixed with a different kind are they nullified in sixty, but if they become mixed with their own kind, they are not nullified even in a thousand. They are: a) davar she-yesh lo matirin (something that will become permitted) (below section 14); b) the wine of gentiles, regarding which there is a concern that it was poured as a libation for idolatry (SA 134:2-3).

And there are forbidden substances that, if they became mixed with a different kind, are nullified in sixty, but if they became mixed with their own kind, since they have a certain severity, are not nullified in sixty but rather in a higher measure. They are: teruma and ḥalla, orla and kilei ha-kerem. The severity of teruma and ḥalla is that one who eats them intentionally is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (above 7, note 10), and therefore the Sages were stringent that they be nullified in a hundred (Mishna Ḥalla 1:9). Their nullification is in a hundred because terumat ma'aser, which renders the produce fit, is one hundredth, and the Sages taught that if it falls back into the ninety-nine parts that remained, it is not nullified, and one would need to treat all the produce according to the law of teruma; but if it falls into a hundred – it is nullified, and the produce is permitted to be eaten by all Israel (except that one must give the kohen the amount of the teruma that fell, since this portion belongs to him).

With orla and kilei ha-kerem the punishment is indeed ordinary (lashes), but their prohibition is more severe, for they are forbidden both for eating and for benefit; therefore the Sages enacted that they be nullified in a double measure – in two hundred (Mishna Orla 2:1; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:13-16).10

notes_en.en: When the mixture is min be-mino, it has an aspect of severity, in that the forbidden substance remains as it was, and therefore it is not nullified. This is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that with all forbidden substances min be-mino is not nullified, because there is no clash between the forbidden and the permitted (as in the words of the Ran cited above in note 2). But when the forbidden substance became mixed with a different kind, if there was sixty times against it, its flavor and its essence are completely nullified (Shakh 102:4). The halakha was ruled according to the Sages, that in a mixture of dry with dry, same kind, the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority, because the clash is between the permitted and the forbidden, and the permitted prevails. Nevertheless, in special cases the aspect of severity of a min be-mino mixture prevails. Therefore, with teruma, orla and kilei ha-kerem, whose prohibition has severity, one hundred or two hundred times is needed to nullify the forbidden substance. And with davar she-yesh lo matirin there is not so much of a clash between the forbidden and the permitted, since the forbidden substance is about to become permitted, and therefore it is not nullified.

sections.body_en:
The Sages enacted that a beriya (a whole creature), such as a worm, is not nullified even in a thousand. Specifically the beriya itself is not nullified, but its flavor is nullified in sixty (Ḥullin 100a). This principle, that a beriya has significance, we learned from the prohibition of eating insects: generally only one who eats a volume of a kezayit of the forbidden substance is punished with lashes, but when the forbidden substance is a beriya, such as an insect, even when it is smaller than a kezayit, one who eats it is punished with lashes (above 23:1).

Four conditions must be met for a forbidden substance to be considered a beriya and not be nullified even in a thousand: a) It must be from the animal kingdom and not the plant kingdom; therefore a grain of wheat does not have the status of a beriya. b) The beriya must be whole; but if part of it was cut off, such as a leg, or it was crushed until its form changed – it does not have the significance of a beriya. c) A whole limb of an animal can also have the status of a beriya, if it has a distinct name and if it were divided – its name would be lost. Therefore the gid ha-nasheh (sciatic nerve) and ever min ha-ḥai (a limb from a living animal) have the status of a beriya, but ḥelev does not have the status of a beriya, because even if it is cut, its name remains ḥelev. d) The status of beriya exists only when the forbidden substance was forbidden from its inception, such as an insect, the gid ha-nasheh or a non-kosher bird; but a kosher bird that died without ritual slaughter does not have the status of a beriya, because its prohibition is not intrinsic, but rather because it died without kosher slaughter (SA 100:1; above 23:4).11

notes_en.en: According to the Rash, Or Zaru'a, Rashba and Kaftor Va-feraḥ, a beriya is nullified in 960. And some say it is nullified in a thousand. According to most Rishonim a beriya is not nullified even in a thousand; this is also the opinion of Tosafot, Ramban, Ra'ah, Rosh, Ritva, Ran and others, and so it was ruled in SA 100:1 (above 23, note 5). However, in situations of doubt one adds the opinion of the lenient authorities, as cited above 23:7, in the second principle. Likewise, one adds the opinion of the Aḥaronim who hold that tiny or repulsive creatures do not have the significance of a beriya (above 23, notes 5; 11-12).

sections.body_en:
Foods that are so especially significant that, because of their great significance, people always count them one by one, are not nullified. The Sages gave examples of this: a special pomegranate called the “pomegranate of Badan” (from Bidan near Elon Moreh), or a special nut called the “nut of Perekh” (from Purikh near Shekhem), large and special cabbage stalks, a large sealed barrel of wine, and likewise anything that is always customarily sold by count because of its significance. But things sold by weight or volume are nullified like other forbidden substances. Likewise, things that are customarily sold by count for the purpose of calculating their price and not because of their significance, such as packages of rice and sugar, cans of preserves and bottles of wine – are nullified like other forbidden substances. An example of a significant item in our day is an especially high-quality bottle of wine or whisky whose price is hundreds of shekels.12

All that the Sages ruled to be stringent regarding significant items, a beriya and a piece fit to serve to an honored guest – that they are not nullified even in a thousand – applies when the mixture remains as it was, for then, because of the significance of the forbidden substance, it is not nullified. But if one of the items in the mixture fell into the sea or became mixed into a non-kosher dish, in a manner that there is no longer any possibility that a Jew will ever eat it, we attribute it, saying that perhaps it was the forbidden item that fell and was lost, and consequently the forbidden substance no longer has extra significance, and it is nullified according to the accepted rules, in a majority or in sixty. However, the Sages added a condition to the permission: that each time one eats from the mixture, he eat two pieces together, and if they are large, that with each eating he eat from both of them together, so that there will always be certainty that one of the pieces he is eating is permitted, and then its companion is drawn after it (Zevaḥim 74a; SA 110:7).13

notes_en.en:
The Sages enacted that extremely significant items are not nullified even in a thousand; however, they disagreed about the definition of their significance, and three opinions were stated on this (Mishna Orla 3:7; Bavli Beitza 3b). a) According to Rabbi Meir as understood by Reish Lakish, “anything whose way is to be counted” (kol she-darko limnot), that is, an item that is generally customarily counted because of its significance – is not nullified; and so ruled the Terumah, Sha'arei Dura and Maharshal. b) According to Rabbi Meir as understood by Rabbi Yoḥanan, “that whose way is to be counted” (et she-darko limnot), that is, only an item that is always customarily counted because of its significance – is not nullified; but if there are times when it is not counted, it is nullified like other forbidden substances. This is the opinion of most Rishonim, among them: Ri, Ritzba, Ran, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, Semag, Semak, Tur and Rema 110:1. c) The Sages in the Mishna enumerated six significant items that are not nullified, and the Rambam explained that they are examples of extremely significant items, and anything as significant as they are, according to the place and time, is not nullified. And so ruled the Rambam and SA 110:1. If so, it emerges that according to the Rambam, the opinion of the Sages is very close to the opinion of those who hold like Rabbi Meir as understood by Rabbi Yoḥanan, and so wrote Arukh Ha-shulḥan 101:4. According to all opinions, items that are customarily counted because it is more convenient to calculate their price that way are not significant, for otherwise even candies that cost a few agorot are sold by count. And so wrote Pri To'ar and Matteh Yehonatan. Thus the three opinions are close to one another, for all agree that it refers to extremely significant items; the question is only how significant they are.
In practice it is difficult to apply the various opinions to our generation. It seems obvious that packages of sugar and rice and bottles of wine are not included among significant items, as evidenced by the fact that they are also sold in cases, so they are not sold one by one. One can also learn this from the fact that a small barrel of wine is not among the seven items, and it is no less significant than the good bottles of wine of our day. In any event, whenever we are in doubt whether something is a significant item, one should be lenient, in accordance with the law of a doubt concerning a rabbinic law. Only when the item is so extremely significant that it is not nullified in one's awareness, whether because of its high price or because of its special quality, is it not nullified.

We attribute [the forbidden piece to the lost one] and permit when the piece fell on its own; but if a Jew dropped it inadvertently, we do not permit, lest he do so intentionally. However, if a Jew inadvertently ate one of the pieces, since there is no concern that he will intentionally eat from the forbidden mixture, we attribute and permit (SA 110:7; Terumat Ha-deshen 175).
Seemingly, according to the rule kol de-parish me-ruba parish (whatever separates, separates from the majority), what fell should be treated as permitted, so how can the mixture be permitted on account of it? The Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit 4:2) explained that the law of kol de-parish applies when the piece that separated is before us, so that there is a necessity to define its status; but when it has been lost, one can attribute it as being the forbidden one, since by Torah law the mixture is permitted, because the forbidden substance is nullified in a majority. His intent is not that we truly estimate that the piece that fell is the forbidden one, but rather that its falling diluted the severity of the significance of the forbidden substance in the mixture, since perhaps what fell was the forbidden one. The Rosh (Ḥullin 7:37) explained that after a piece fell from the mixture, a sfek sfeka (double doubt) was created: a doubt whether perhaps the piece that fell was forbidden, and if not, perhaps the piece the person is eating is not forbidden. And the Rema wrote that the entire permission after the piece fell is on condition that the mixture is eaten by two people, not at the same time. Many Aḥaronim were not concerned about his words (Pri Ḥadash, Gra).

sections.title_en: A Piece Fit to Serve to an Honored Guest
sections.body_en:
The Sages established that a piece fit to serve to an honored guest is not nullified even in a thousand, because owing to its great significance, even when it is mixed in sixty it is not nullified in a person's awareness. A piece fit to serve to an honored guest is a piece that can be served to an honored guest as the main part of the meal, so that he will be satisfied from it together with bread or rice and the like. Everything depends on the time and place: there were periods when people customarily honored a guest with a medium piece of meat or a medium piece of hard cheese, because they would then eat a lot of bread with the meat or the cheese, and together with the bread they were customarily satisfied by them. But in our day, when food is more abundant, a piece fit to serve to an honored guest must be at least a quarter of a large chicken, or beef of that size. And when there is a doubt whether the piece is fit to serve to an honored guest, since this law is rabbinic, one is lenient and treats it like other forbidden substances.14

Some say that only a piece that can be served to a guest as it is, is considered fit to serve to an honored guest; but if its cooking was not completed, or it is too large, its law is like that of other forbidden substances (Ran; SA 101:3). And although many Rishonim and Aḥaronim are stringent even while it is raw and large, since the basis of this law is rabbinic, in a pressing situation one may rely on the lenient opinions.15

Even when the piece is forbidden by rabbinic law, if it is fit to serve to an honored guest – it is not nullified. And the entire stringency of a “piece fit to serve to an honored guest” applies on condition that the piece is forbidden in itself, like non-kosher meat, or meat that was cooked with milk. But if it became forbidden because it absorbed forbidden flavor, for example it was cooked with non-kosher gravy, since the forbidden substance itself is not fit to serve to an honored guest, the law of the piece is like that of other forbidden substances (SA and Rema 101:2). If the pieces were cut until they are no longer fit to serve to an honored guest, the forbidden substance once again becomes nullified like other forbidden substances (SA 101:6).

notes_en.en: We learned in Ḥullin 100a that a piece fit to serve to guests, because of its significance, is considered like items that are always customarily counted, and therefore the Sages enacted that it is not nullified even in a thousand. Indeed, main courses served to honored guests are always customarily counted. The intent is not that the ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed is the only food eaten in the meal, and that one becomes fully satisfied from it alone, for people always ate bread with meat or fish, and so wrote Rav Pe'alim (vol. 1 YD 23). Rather the intent is that it is the only main course from which one is satisfied, together with the accepted accompaniments. Admittedly, we find discussions among the poskim regarding the size and quality of a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed, but since it is agreed that everything depends on the time and place (Shakh 101:12-13), one can say that there is no dispute in this. In times when food was abundant – the ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed was larger and people ate less bread with it; and in times of scarcity – the ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed was small and people ate more bread with it. Nowadays we merit abundant food, to the point that many do not eat bread; in any case, the ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed is not the entire meal but the main part of the meal, such as a respectable quarter chicken eaten together with rice and salads. But if the meal includes two courses, it is no longer possible that there is a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed there, since the ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed is one piece that is the main part of the meal.

There are four opinions regarding the law of a piece that after preparation will be fit to serve to an honored guest: a) According to the Rosh, even a slaughtered chicken in its feathers is considered a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed. b) According to Rabbeinu Tam, a chicken in its feathers requires too much preparation, but a large, raw piece of meat is a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed. And so ruled the Rema 101:3. c) According to the Rashba, a raw piece of meat of the appropriate size is considered a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed, but if it is too large it is not. d) According to the Ran, only a cooked piece of a size appropriate to serve to guests now is considered a ḥatikha ha-re'uya le-hitkabed, and so it was ruled in SA 101:3. However, the Pri Ḥadash remarked that from SA 69:14 and 105:9 it emerges that even a raw piece is fit to serve to an honored guest. And so ruled the Radbaz, Arukh Ha-shulḥan, Pri To'ar and Ziv'ḥei Tzedek. However, since the law is rabbinic, many of those who follow the view of the SA ruled to be lenient, among them: Shulḥan Gavoha, Sho'el Ve-nish'al, Yabi'a Omer 5, YD 8. And since the law is rabbinic, in a pressing situation members of all communities may rely on the lenient opinions.

sections.title_en: It Is Forbidden to Nullify Forbidden Substances
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to nullify forbidden substances, whether by mixing nevela gravy into kosher gravy that is sixty times greater than it, or by mixing a piece of nevela meat with two kosher pieces like it. For since the Torah forbade eating them, it is forbidden to bring about a situation in which they will be nullified in a majority or in sixty and be eaten contrary to the intent of the Torah. Even if nevela gravy already became mixed into kosher gravy that did not contain sixty times against it, it is forbidden to add more water in order to nullify it in sixty. Likewise, if a piece of nevela meat and a piece of kosher meat became mixed, it is forbidden to add another permitted piece in order to nullify the forbidden substance in a majority. Likewise, if the mixture consisted of pieces fit to serve to an honored guest, or of especially significant items that are not nullified, it is forbidden to cut them up and cancel their significance so that the forbidden substance will be nullified in a majority or in sixty.

If one transgressed and nullified the forbidden substance: if he did so inadvertently – the forbidden substance is nullified. And if he did so intentionally – it is forbidden for him and for those for whom he did it to benefit from it, but for others the mixture is permitted (Mishna Terumot 5:9; Beitza 4b; Gittin 54b; SA 99:5).

However, if the forbidden substance that became mixed in is forbidden only by rabbinic law, and the kosher foods do not contain a sufficient quantity to nullify it, the Sages permitted adding to it in order to nullify it. Likewise, if it is a significant item that is not nullified – it is permitted to cut up the pieces in the mixture in order to nullify it (Rambam; SA 99:6). And some are stringent even when the prohibition is rabbinic (Rosh, Rema). And in a pressing situation, even those who follow their view may be lenient (Pri Megadim, Rabbi Akiva Eiger).

It is permitted to grind wheat intended for flour that has many insects mixed into it which are difficult to remove, and through the grinding the insects will be cut up and nullified in sixty. This is because the intent is not to nullify the forbidden substance but to grind the wheat into flour, and incidentally the forbidden substance is nullified (Taz 137:4).16

notes_en.en:
Some say that it is forbidden by Torah law to nullify forbidden substances (Ra'avad, Ra'ah, Ra'avan, Pri To'ar). And some say that the prohibition is rabbinic (Ran, Ra'avya, Rama Mi-Fano, Pri Megadim, Ḥokhmat Adam). And some say that with a “dry” forbidden substance the prohibition is from the Torah, since it stands on its own, and with a “liquid” one that blended and was nullified, the prohibition is rabbinic (Noda Bi-Yehuda, Ḥatam Sofer). According to all opinions, with substances forbidden for benefit the prohibition is from the Torah (Ḥavot Da'at). It seems that the dispute is not polar, and all agree that one who nullifies a forbidden substance acts contrary to the intent of the Torah, which commanded not to eat a forbidden substance, while he contrives a way by which he will eat the forbidden substance. They disagreed only whether he thereby transgresses a full Torah prohibition, or whether it is only contrary to the intent of the Torah, in the category of naval bi-rshut ha-Torah (“a scoundrel within the bounds of the Torah”) (see Ramban, Vayikra 19:2).
In Beitza 4b we learned that if muktzeh wood fell into an oven on Yom Tov, and there is not a majority of non-muktzeh wood there, it is permitted to add non-muktzeh wood to it in order to nullify it in a majority, so as to burn it and cook the festive meal with it. According to the Rambam and Rashba, it is forbidden le-khatḥila to nullify a rabbinic prohibition, but if it became mixed in, it is permitted to add in order to nullify it. And so wrote SA 99:6; Pri Ḥadash, and all the Sephardic poskim. According to Tosafot, the permission applies only to a rabbinic prohibition that has no basis in the Torah, like muktzeh. According to the Rosh, Ra'ah and Ran, the permission applies only when the forbidden substance is consumed before one benefits from it, such as the wood that is burned in order to cook with it for the meal; but when the forbidden substance is not consumed, it is forbidden to nullify even rabbinic prohibitions. And so ruled the Rema and most Ashkenazic poskim. And some Ashkenazic poskim ruled leniently in accordance with the opinion of the SA, among them: Maharshal and Taz. According to Pri Megadim, Siftei Da'at 17, and Responsa Rabbi Akiva Eiger 38, even according to the Rema, in a pressing situation or in a case of great loss, one may be lenient in accordance with the SA. Admittedly, some are stringent even in a case of great loss (Ḥokhmat Adam), but since it is a doubt concerning a rabbinic law, and this is the practice of all those who follow the view of the SA and some of the poskim who follow the Rema, this is how one should rule.
When there were creeping creatures in the wheat, and the effort to sort them out is enormous, it is permitted to grind it into flour and nullify the creatures in it in sixty, for a crushed beriya is nullified in sixty. And although it is forbidden to nullify a forbidden substance le-khatḥila, when one intends in any case to grind the wheat into flour, and has no interest in the ground creatures, this is not considered intending to nullify the forbidden substance (Rabbi Akiva Eiger YD 77, and so it is implied by Taz 137:4).

sections.body_en:
A davar she-yesh lo matirin (something that will become permitted), that is, a forbidden food whose prohibition will lapse over time and it will become permitted, or that can be permitted through a simple action, which became mixed with its own kind – the Sages established that it is not nullified even in a thousand. Therefore, wheat that is forbidden under the prohibition of ḥadash (new grain before the omer offering) that became mixed with wheat from the previous year – even if the permitted wheat is a thousand times the forbidden, all of it is forbidden until the day of the omer, when the prohibition of ḥadash lapses. Likewise, produce of ma'aser sheni and hekdesh (consecrated property) that became mixed with other produce is not nullified, since it can be permitted by redeeming it with money (Nedarim 58a).

This is because the whole matter of nullifying forbidden substances in a majority or in sixty is be-di'avad, when one is forced to decide the status of the mixture; but if the forbidden substance is about to become permitted, whether through the passage of time or through an action that will permit it, instead of overpowering it by force and nullifying it, one should wait until it becomes permitted. All this is on condition that the forbidden substance is still noticeable in our awareness, that is, it became mixed with its own kind, and then, even though there is sixty times against it, the forbidden substance has not changed and its name remains as it was. But if the davar she-yesh lo matirin became mixed with a different kind, and there is sixty times against it, it is nullified by virtue of its extreme smallness, for its name and its flavor have vanished from the world, and therefore there is no need to wait until it becomes permitted (SA 102:1).

A rabbinic prohibition that will become permitted is also not nullified. Therefore, an egg laid on Yom Tov, which is forbidden as muktzeh until the conclusion of Yom Tov, that became mixed with a thousand eggs – all the eggs are forbidden until the conclusion of Yom Tov (Beitza 4b).

If by the time the permitted time arrives the flavor of the food will be spoiled, it is not considered a davar she-yesh lo matirin. But if it will deteriorate a little, in a manner that is not very noticeable, the forbidden substance is considered a davar she-yesh lo matirin and is not nullified (SA 102:4; Kreti 12).

If a utensil that absorbed forbidden flavor became mixed up with permitted utensils, since there is effort involved in performing hagala on all the utensils, it is not considered a davar she-yesh lo matirin. However, one should wait until a full day passes over the utensil that absorbed the forbidden substance, for then its flavor will be spoiled and by Torah law there will be no prohibition in it (Rashba; SA 102:3). And if they can easily be kashered by hagala, some say that even after a full day one must permit them through hagala (Shakh 8, based on the Maharil).17

notes_en.en:
The nullification of forbidden substances and the need to decide a doubt are be-di'avad, for le-khatḥila one should eat foods that have no doubt or mixture of a forbidden substance. Therefore, when the forbidden substance will become permitted, since it will become permitted in any case, the Sages ruled to wait until it becomes permitted on its own (Rashi, Beitza 3b). However, if the forbidden substance became mixed with a different kind, even though it will become permitted, it is nullified according to the regular rules (Yerushalmi Nedarim 6:4). This is because in such a situation the entire mixture is called by the name of the permitted kind, and the forbidden substance that became mixed in it has been nullified and has faded from awareness. And even though it will become permitted, one should not pile on concerns when the name of the forbidden substance has already been forgotten. And as the Ran explained, the power to nullify a forbidden substance stems from the clash created between it and the permitted, and what was said, that a davar she-yesh lo matirin is not nullified, applies when the clash between them is weak (above, note 2). According to the Rema (102:4), if the forbidden substance dissolved completely in the mixture, so that it is not present in its original form at all, even if it will become permitted – it is nullified, and all the more so when the mixture is liquid. On the other hand, according to the Shakh 9, even if the forbidden flavor came out of a forbidden piece and the piece was removed from the mixture, since it is min be-mino and it will become permitted – it is not nullified. And so it is implied by the words of the SA. Where it would prevent the joy of Yom Tov, one may be lenient (MB 513:8; Ziv'ḥei Tzedek YD 102:13). The kind is determined by the name (Shakh 102:3).
One who forbids something to himself by a vow from which he can be released, and it became mixed with other foods – it is not nullified, since he can seek release from it (Rema 102:4; SA 216:10).
The SA YD 102:1 wrote that even a doubtful forbidden substance that became mixed with a permitted one, if it will become permitted – is not nullified. Therefore, even when an egg regarding which there is a doubt whether it was laid on Yom Tov became mixed with a thousand, it is not nullified. However, some permit it because of sfek sfeka, and the SA OḤ 513:2 inclined to this. And in a case of loss one may be lenient (MB 5).

sections.title_en: Ḥatikha Na'aseit Nevela (ḤaNaN) with Meat and Milk
sections.body_en:
When milk became mixed with meat and was cooked with it, both became entirely forbidden, that is, the entire piece became forbidden, and in the language of the Sages: ḥatikha na'aseit nevela (“the piece becomes nevela”), abbreviated ḤaNaN. For example, if 10 ml (milliliters) of milk fell onto a piece of meat of 90 ml, since the milk imparted flavor to the meat, the entire piece, which now measures 100 ml, becomes nevela. Therefore, if this piece fell into a meat dish of five liters, the entire dish becomes forbidden, because one does not calculate the milk alone; rather, the entire piece, whose volume is 100 ml, is considered nevela, and since the dish does not contain sixty times more than it, but only fifty times – all of it becomes forbidden. If those five liters that became nevela fell into a huge meat dish whose volume is 250 liters, all of it becomes forbidden, since it contains only fifty times against the five liters that became nevela. Thus those 10 ml of milk rendered forbidden, through a gradual process, a quantity of meat 25,000 times greater than themselves. If those 250 liters of meat were mixed into 250 pots, a liter into each pot, with each pot containing 50 liters of meat, all the mixtures became forbidden. Thus those 10 ml of milk rendered forbidden a quantity of meat 1,250,000 times greater than themselves. In this way one could continue and render forbidden all the meat that exists in the world, for as long as the mixture does not contain sixty times more than the forbidden substance, the entire mixture becomes forbidden and turns into an entirely forbidden substance. But if from the start, the first time, the meat had contained sixty times the 10 ml of milk that fell into it, the milk would have been nullified in sixty, and all these mixtures would have been kosher.

One can learn a moral idea from this halakha: as long as one does not succeed in nullifying evil, one should distance oneself from it, for otherwise it can corrupt and render everything forbidden through a gradual process. However, the distancing is for a short time, for over time the forbidden food deteriorates and its flavor becomes spoiled, and it can no longer render forbidden.18

notes_en.en:
It is explained in the Gemara (Ḥullin 108a) that if it were possible to squeeze out all the milk absorbed in the meat, according to Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, Shmuel and Reish Lakish the meat would return to its permitted status, and consequently a piece does not become nevela. Whereas according to Rabbi Ḥanina, Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan, the meat would remain forbidden, because after the milk and meat were cooked together the piece becomes nevela. And this is the opinion of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim (Rambam, Ramban, Rashba, Ran and others). (The Ra'avad has a different opinion: everything we learned regarding the law of ḤaNaN is according to the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda regarding min be-mino, which is not nullified even in a thousand; but the halakha does not follow him, and consequently when there is sixty times against the first milk that fell, it will be nullified.)
The halakha was ruled that ḥatikha na'aseit nevela (Tur and SA 92:3). This law is from the Torah, because it is a scriptural decree that if meat and milk are cooked together they are forbidden, and one who eats a kezayit of them is liable to lashes. And some explained that since one who cooks them transgresses a Torah prohibition, they are included in the negative commandment “You shall not eat any abomination” (Devarim 14:3), about which the Sages said (Ḥullin 114b): “Whatever I have made abominable to you is under ‘you shall not eat’”; and even if they are separated, they remain in their abomination and prohibition (Beit Meir 92:4, based on Knesset Ha-gedola).
When the prohibition of meat and milk is rabbinic, some say that the law of ḤaNaN does not apply to it, for it is enough that the Sages forbade it, and one should not decree the law of ḤaNaN upon it (Rambam; SA 99:6; Pri Ḥadash; Arukh Ha-shulḥan). And some say that since each of the kinds is kosher and they became forbidden only through their mixture, the law of ḤaNaN is applied to them (Rashba); and furthermore, the Sages made their measures uniform, just as they enacted the law of ḤaNaN for all forbidden substances, as explained in the next halakha (Ran, Maharshal, Baḥ, Taz and Shakh).
The poskim disagreed regarding a case in which only meat flavor, without a trace of milk, was expelled from the piece that became nevela. For example, a pot containing pieces of meat with gravy at its bottom, and milk fell onto one of the pieces lying entirely above the gravy, and it became forbidden: according to the Ran and the Shakh (92:7; 105:17), if the piece was fatty and meat flavor came out of it into the other pieces, even though it is clear that no milk flavor came out – for milk is by nature lean, and without being steeped in gravy it does not come out of the piece of meat in which it was absorbed – all the pieces become forbidden, because even the meat flavor alone is forbidden, since the piece became nevela. By contrast, according to Tosafot, the Terumah, Rashba, Rema and Taz (92:7; 105:13), even though if all the milk were removed from the piece of meat it would remain forbidden, when only meat flavor comes out of the forbidden piece into the other pieces, they are permitted, since only meat flavor came out into them. And this is the opinion of most Rishonim and Aḥaronim, among them: Maharshal, Pri Ḥadash and Gra.

sections.title_en: Ḥatikha Na'aseit Nevela (ḤaNaN) with Other Forbidden Substances
sections.body_en:
It is agreed that when meat became mixed with milk through cooking, the entire piece becomes nevela, for the meat alone is kosher, and the milk alone is kosher, and through their being mixed both became forbidden; thus the entire piece becomes nevela by Torah law, and if it falls into another dish that does not contain sixty times against it, the entire dish becomes forbidden. But the Rishonim disagreed regarding other forbidden substances that became mixed into kosher foods. For example, if 10 ml (milliliters) of blood became mixed into 90 ml of kosher meat, it is clear that the piece of meat mixed with blood is forbidden to eat; the question is whether it is considered nevela.

Some say that although the meat is forbidden to eat because of the blood mixed in it, it did not become nevela; therefore, if this forbidden piece of meat falls into another dish of 1,000 ml (a liter), since there is more than sixty times the forbidden blood there – the dish is kosher. However, the piece itself that originally absorbed the blood is forbidden, because it is possible that the blood remained in it and did not spread throughout the dish (Rabbeinu Efrayim, Rosh, SA 92:4).

And some say that the Sages made the laws of other forbidden substances the same as the law of meat and milk, and established that with other forbidden substances, too, ḥatikha na'aseit nevela; and since the blood rendered the piece of meat forbidden, the entire piece of meat became nevela, and if it fell into a dish that does not contain sixty times it, the entire dish is forbidden (Rabbeinu Tam, Ramban, Ran and Rema).19

notes_en.en:
According to Rabbeinu Efrayim (Tosafot 100a, s.v. be-she-kadam), Rashba, Rosh and SA 92:4, the law of ḤaNaN does not apply to other forbidden substances, and so ruled the Aḥaronim of Sephardic origin (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 92:22). And according to Rashi, Rabbeinu Tam, Ri, Ramban, Ra'ah, Ra'avya, Ran, Or Zaru'a, the Terumah, Semag, Semak, Mordekhai and Rema, the law of ḤaNaN applies to other forbidden substances (according to the Ran, Taz, Shakh and most poskim it is rabbinic, and according to the Mahari Kolon and those who concur with him it is from the Torah).
According to the lenient view, that piece remains forbidden, because perhaps the forbidden flavor in it did not spread throughout the mixture (Rashba and most poskim). And some say that since it was cooked with other foods, the forbidden flavor spread through everything, and the piece that was originally forbidden returns to its permitted status (Tur).
According to the stringent view: some say that ḤaNaN applies even to rabbinic prohibitions (Taz, Pri Megadim, Kreti, Minḥat Yaakov), and some are lenient that ḤaNaN does not apply to rabbinic prohibitions (Pri Ḥadash, Arukh Ha-shulḥan). In time of need one may be lenient (Ktav Sofer YD 52; Igrot Moshe YD 2:36). They disagreed whether ḤaNaN applies to part of a piece, such as the amount requiring removal (kedei netila), as cited in Shakh 96:9. And one may be lenient by adding the opinion of the SA.
ḤaNaN in liquids: With liquid meat and milk, such as meat fat and milk, it is agreed that the law of ḤaNaN applies, since each alone is kosher and only through their combination did they become forbidden, and therefore their entire mixture became nevela (Ramban, Rashba and Shakh 92:15). But they disagreed regarding other forbidden substances. Some say that only a solid piece becomes nevela, since it has significance because it is recognizable as a forbidden piece, and even if it falls into another dish, the forbidden substance absorbed in it will not spread evenly throughout the dish, but will remain more within it. But with liquids ḤaNaN does not apply, because all the liquids mix with one another again evenly, and a new mixture is created (Ramban, Mordekhai). And some say that ḤaNaN applies to liquids as well (Tosafot Ḥullin 100a, s.v. be-she-kadam). In practice, according to the stringent view, le-khatḥila one takes into account and is stringent even with liquids and without cooking, and in a case of great loss one may be lenient with liquids (Rema 92:4, Noda Bi-Yehuda, Pri Megadim and Ḥokhmat Adam). (According to the Ran and Maharshal, when the mixture was created through cooking, ḤaNaN applies even to liquids, and if without cooking, ḤaNaN does not apply even to a piece, because the basis of the law of ḤaNaN in other forbidden substances is learned from the prohibition of cooking meat with milk; and in time of need it is proper to add their opinion in order to be lenient.)

sections.title_en: The Rules of Kamma Kamma Batel and Ḥozer Ve-ni'or
sections.body_en:
A question arose regarding a case in which a forbidden substance fell into a permitted one and was nullified, and afterwards another forbidden substance fell into the permitted food, and the permitted food contains a sufficient measure to nullify it, but if we combine it with the first forbidden substance that was nullified before, the permitted food does not contain a sufficient measure to nullify them. According to the rule kamma kamma batel (“the first, the first is nullified”), the first forbidden substance was nullified and can no longer combine with the second forbidden substance, for whenever there was knowledge between the falling of the first forbidden substance and the falling of the second forbidden substance – they do not combine. This is because at the time the matter became known, the permitted overpowered the forbidden and nullified it, and it can no longer combine with a forbidden substance that falls afterwards. On the other hand, according to the rule ḥozer ve-ni'or (“it reawakens”), the first forbidden substance reawakens and combines with the forbidden substance that has now fallen into the mixture, and if the permitted food does not contain a sufficient quantity to nullify both of them together, the entire mixture is forbidden.
